message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
These are written from recall, without re-checking the text. Phrases in quotation marks are ones I believe are close to verbatim; everything else is paraphrase.

**Title and opening**
- The title is "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team."
- The note is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because ordinary good practice is what slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a confident colleague is in the room.

**§1 Receive each claim at the weight it earned**
- Claims come from papers, colleagues, summaries and your own earlier notes.
- Don't give a claim more weight because it is fluent, comes from someone senior, or confirms what you hoped.
- Don't give it less because it is inconvenient, comes from someone junior, or because doubting feels rigorous.
- Ask what supports a claim, how directly, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong.
- A well-measured result from a controlled comparison is heavy.
- A mechanism suggested after the data were in is light but not nothing. Note it and say what would test it.
- "Confidence is information about the speaker, not about the world."
- Inflation is easy to spot afterwards. Deflation is harder, because a caveat on a sound result looks careful but is a misreport.
- Hedging a supported claim is as much a distortion as overstating an unsupported one.
- Example: a supplier's defect rate fell after a process change. Three months of the supplier's own figures deserve light weight. A year of your own incoming inspection shouldn't be buried under "it may be noise."

**§2 Take in what was said before you answer**
- Restate the substance briefly, in your own terms.
- This is not politeness. It is how both sides check they received the same thing.
- The part you don't restate is the part most likely to drop.
- Answering the three easy points and skipping the hard fourth means answering a different, easier message.
- If you can't restate something, you haven't understood it, and your next move is a question.
- Then move on. The restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The contribution is the implication, the gap, or the next test.
- Example: a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. Restate all five, answer four, and say the budget question needs figures you don't yet have and when you'll have them.

**§3 Go to the source**
- Summaries, abstracts, notes and memory are compressions. They lose the details that matter: the denominator, the subgroup, the condition under which the result held.
- Check against the primary material when a decision depends on a specific.
- This applies most to things you think you already know, because claims you've repeated to yourself drift.
- The source is the referee. Agreement among colleagues is not.
- A team that checks claims against each other instead of the data can drift together into a shared mistake that no one inside it can see.
- Example: you remember a report as saying "costs fell 12%," but it said costs per unit fell 12% while volume fell 20%. Open it before the budget meeting.

**§4 Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed**
- Closing early feels like progress, but it turns uncertainty into a false fact that others build on.
- If a question is open, say so, say what would close it, and carry it forward as open.
- Keeping a settled question open, out of discomfort or because one more check feels safer, wastes effort and signals unwarranted doubt.
- Example: a new form reduced errors at two sites, but the busiest site has a different workflow. Report the first as found and the second as open, not as "promising" and "likely."

**§5 Value the colleague who sees differently**
- A colleague's most useful contribution is what you couldn't produce yourself.
- A reviewer who knows what you know mostly returns what you already see. Difference is the source of new information.
- Give reviewers the material and the question, not your conclusion, your worries, or what you hope they'll find.
- Telling a fresh reader what you think removes the difference that made them worth asking.
- In reverse: when you are the fresh reader, read first, form your view, then look at what others concluded.
- Raise objections. One held back because the room seems settled is information the team doesn't get.

**§6 Make your moves where they can be seen**
- When you can see the right next step, take it visibly so others can check and reverse it.
- Share drafts before they feel finished, make the call and show your reasoning, and push the result.
- Asking permission for a decision the evidence settles hands it to someone with less context. It also stalls the work on your guess about their reply.
- Your guess about a colleague's response is your own model of them and contains nothing new. Only a real move gets a real reply.
- This is not licence to act without regard to others. Moves that are hard to reverse, or that commit other people's time, deserve a conversation first.
- Most moves are reversible, and the default for those is to make them openly.
- Example: don't ask "should I restructure section three?" Restructure it in a copy, explain the change, and invite reversal.

**§7 Failures come in pairs**
- Inflating a claim / deflating a claim.
- Inventing a flaw / inventing a reassurance.
- Closing too early / keeping open too long.
- Killing a live line / keeping a dead one.
- Deferring / dismissing (accepting or rejecting a claim because of who made it).
- Offloading / overriding.
- If you're correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.

**A last word**
- It is not a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes careful work when it goes well, and you will mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the work itself: the source that overrules you, the colleague who reads differently, the result that doesn't come out as expected.
- Welcome those, because they are how you find out what you didn't already know.

The text is still in my context, so I can't prove I recalled rather than reread it. If you're testing recall, the useful check is to compare this list against the original for drift, especially the examples and the exact wording of the quotations.
